cues.text: A Calendar Drifting Out of Step
By the sixteenth century, the Julian calendar had drifted noticeably out of alignment with the actual solar year.
In use across the Christian West since Julius Caesar's reforms in 46 BC, its estimate of the year's length ran roughly eleven minutes too long.
The error was small in any single year but had accumulated, over sixteen centuries, into a discrepancy of about ten days.

The practical consequence troubled the Church directly: the spring equinox, which the Council of Nicaea in 325 had used to help fix the date of Easter, had slipped noticeably earlier than the calendar itself indicated.
A Commission of Astronomers
Pope Gregory XIII , building on decades of astronomical and calendrical study commissioned by his predecessors, convened a panel of scholars to devise a correction.
He relied above all on calculations by the Italian astronomer and physician Aloysius Lilius , who had died shortly before the reform's adoption.
He also relied on the Jesuit mathematician Christopher Clavius , who refined and defended Lilius's proposal and became the reform's chief public advocate.
Ten Days Removed, A New Leap Rule
On February 24, 1582, Gregory promulgated the bull Inter Gravissimas , decreeing that ten days be removed from the calendar outright.
In Catholic countries, October 4, 1582, was followed directly by October 15.

The bull introduced a refined leap-year rule, exempting century years not evenly divisible by 400 from the usual pattern, keeping the calendar accurate to within about one day every three thousand years.
A Reform Adopted Unevenly
Catholic states adopted the new Gregorian calendar promptly, but Protestant and Orthodox territories resisted for generations, wary of a reform issued by papal authority.
England and its colonies did not adopt it until 1752, Russia not until 1918, and the Eastern Orthodox Church has never adopted it for its own liturgical reckoning.
This divergence still produces differing dates on which Eastern and Western Christians celebrate Easter and Christmas in many years.
Legacy
Despite this uneven and often politically fraught reception, the Gregorian calendar gradually became the civil calendar of virtually the entire world.
Today, it stands as one of the most universally adopted reforms any pope has ever issued, originally aimed at keeping Easter properly anchored to the spring equinox.
It has long since outgrown its religious origin, becoming the ordinary, secular measure of time by which the whole modern world now organizes its years.
